The horse, the banner, the Capitol: a picture of who the procession wanted to look like. Wells’s decision to leave the “rear contingent” is the part the program does not print. Color official program cover for the Woman Suffrage Procession, Washington, D.C., 3 March 1913, showing a woman on horseback before the Capitol. The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920. It did not undo Jim Crow. Many Black women in the South were still blocked by poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence. The amendment changed the federal text. The ground did not change with it. The same years, elsewhere: Qiu Jin 秋瑾 (1875–1907). She unbound her feet, studied in Japan, edited 中國女報 (the Chinese Women’s Journal), and was executed after the 1907 Anqing uprising. Her public life does not sit on the Anglo-American staircase from Seneca Falls to 1920. It belongs in the same decades anyway — a woman deciding she would count in public, under a different state, and paying for it. People Four lives the frame has to stretch for Sojourner Truth c. 1797–1883 Born enslaved in New York. She sold cartes-de-visite captioned “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” The card was a living. It was also an argument about who owned the image of a woman who had been treated as property. Carte-de-visite, 1864. “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” Ida B. Wells 1862–1931 Anti-lynching journalist; Southern Horrors appeared in 1892. She treated suffrage and racial terror as one fight, which is why a segregated parade order was not a small slight. She walked into the Illinois line instead. Ida B. Wells-Barnett, photograph by Mary Garrity, c. 1893. Inez Milholland 1886–1916 Lawyer and the image the 1913 procession needed at its head. She died in 1916 on a western suffrage tour, at thirty. The photograph outlived the campaign she was riding for. The 1913 visual: white cape, white horse, Pennsylvania Avenue. Qiu Jin 秋瑾 1875–1907 Unbound feet. Study in Japan. Editor of 中國女報. Executed after the 1907 Anqing uprising. If “first wave” cannot hold her, the phrase is too small — not her life. Qiu Jin, photographed between 1900 and 1907. A story The shadow and the substance Sojourner Truth, 1864. She sold the card because lectures did not pay enough. She also put her own copyright on it. Sojourner Truth’s 1864 carte-de-visite, with the printed line I sell the shadow to support the substance under her portrait. Truth sold her image because lectures did not pay enough. The “shadow” is the photograph — a thing that can be reproduced, captioned, passed from hand to hand. The “substance” is the work, and the body that had been treated as property. She put the sentence on the card in English, under her own name, and made the sale part of the argument: I will be paid for the copy of me that you can hold. Keep the card in mind when a movement talks about “women” as if the category were already settled. Someone is always deciding which body is the subject, and which body is the illustration. After The vote, the doldrums, and the staircase In the United States the 1920s through the 1950s are often called the “doldrums”: the vote arrived, the coalition thinned. The word is a weather report written after the fact. It describes a particular organized feminism going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended. What gets called the second wave — the 1960s and 1970s — turned to the workplace, to sexuality, to housework. “The personal is political.” The who-counts problem returned in public, including in the Combahee River Collective statement of 1977, which refused to treat race, sex, and class as separate queues. The wave metaphor itself is the after. It offers a tidy staircase: first the vote, then the rest. It hides the people who were never on the stairs — and the fights that did not wait for the next numbered swell. A question Leave this on the table When a movement says “we,” who is being asked to wait? Time to Remember — Time of the Suffragettes (1911–1913) British Pathé compilation of British suffragette newsreel, 1911–1913. This is not film of the 1913 Washington procession. The Derby — 1912 & 1913 British Pathé racing newsreel. It includes the 1913 Epsom Derby, when Emily Wilding Davison stepped onto the course. Again: Britain, not Pennsylvania Avenue.
